title: ‘Unguarded moments’: a lost archive of street photography – in pictures
text:
‘Unguarded moments’: a lost archive of street photography – in pictures
Little-known photographer John Baer captured everyday life before putting down his camera in 1954. His son discovered the images decades later after his death, and John Baer: The Extraordinary Ordinary / A Memoir in Photographs, 1945–1954 marks their first public release
In January 1942, when Baer was serving as the managing editor of the campus newspaper at Pennsylvania State University, he was drafted to fight in the second world war
In 1948, Baer and his wife, Louise, moved from Europe to New York City, where they rented a fifth-floor walk-up at 215 Second Avenue in the East Village
In 1950, he and his wife sublet their New York City apartment to move to Montpellier, France, where he photographed daily life, friends and political posters that warned against American military and economic dominance
During Christmas 1959, he invited Kurt, a German soldier, to his home for dinner. When his son, Andrew Baer, asked him if Kurt helped the Nazis, he responded that if he had been born in Germany, he also would have been in the German army.
As his son Andrew Baer writes in John Baer: The Extraordinary Ordinary / A Memoir in Photographs, 1945–1954, “John’s ability to quietly blend in allowed him to catch people in unguarded moments, and from surprising angles”
In 1952, shortly after Andrew was born, he and Louise moved from Manhattan to Brooklyn, where he became involved with the group called the Abingdon Square Painters, where he grew his circle of artist and writer friends
Baer and Barney Weinberg, a close friend from Penn State, were the first non-painters to show their work in Abingdon Square’s West Village gallery. His installation series Stuyvesant Town placed groups of unframed prints on large, horizontal boards to create high-contrast compositions, which were unconventional for the time
In 1960, he moved back to Hastings-on-Hudson after remarrying Louise. They then moved to Manhattan and Rhode Island before divorcing again in 1986. Since then, his images have largely gone untouched and been unseen until now
